theoryAdd.text: Going Deeper: Charge, Power and Energy

Current can be linked to the motion of the individual charge carriers. Suppose a conductor of area A contains n free electrons per cubic metre, each drifting with an average velocity v. In a time t every electron within a length vt of the wire, that is nAvt electrons, crosses a given section, carrying a charge nAvte. Dividing by t gives the current, I = nAev. For copper n ≈ 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³, so 2 A in a 2.5 mm² wire corresponds to a drift speed of only about 0.06 mm/s.

theoryAdd.latex: I = n A e v_d, \qquad Q = It, \qquad N = \frac{Q}{e}
theoryAdd.plainText: I = n A e v_d ; Q = I t ; number of electrons N = Q/e

theoryAdd.text: The drift speed is tiny, yet a lamp lights the instant the switch is closed. This is because the conductor is already full of free electrons: closing the switch sets up the electric field along the whole circuit almost at the speed of light, and every electron everywhere starts drifting at once. Energy is carried by the field, not by electrons travelling from the source to the load.

When a practical source of EMF E and internal resistance r feeds a load R, the current is I = E/(R + r) and the terminal voltage is V = ER/(R + r). The source generates power EI, of which I²R reaches the load and I²r is wasted as heat inside the source. The fraction delivered, V/E = R/(R + r), is the efficiency of the source; it approaches 100% when R is much larger than r. When a battery is being charged, current is forced into its positive terminal and the charger must supply V = E + Ir.

theoryAdd.plainText: I = E/(R + r); efficiency η = I²R/(EI) = V/E = R/(R + r)

theoryAdd.text:
Worked example 1 - battery feeding a load
E = 12 V, r = 0.4 ohm, load R = 5.6 ohm
Step 1: I = E / (R + r) = 12 / 6.0 = 2 A
Step 2: terminal voltage V = E - I r = 12 - 2 x 0.4 = 11.2 V
Step 3: power generated = E I = 12 x 2 = 24 W
Step 4: power to load = I^2 R = 4 x 5.6 = 22.4 W; loss inside = I^2 r = 1.6 W
Step 5: efficiency = 22.4 / 24 = 93.3 %  (= R / (R + r) = 5.6 / 6)

Worked example 2 - heating water and the cost of energy
10 kg of water is heated from 15 C to 65 C by a 2 kW, 230 V heater, efficiency 90 %.
c(water) = 4200 J/(kg C), tariff Rs 10 per kWh
Step 1: heat needed = m c dT = 10 x 4200 x 50 = 2.1 MJ
Step 2: electrical input = 2.1 MJ / 0.9 = 2.333 MJ
Step 3: in kWh: 2.333e6 / 3.6e6 = 0.648 kWh
Step 4: time = energy / power = 2.333e6 / 2000 = 1167 s = 19.4 min
Step 5: cost = 0.648 x 10 = Rs 6.48; current = 2000 / 230 = 8.70 A

Circuit analysis uses the passive sign convention to decide whether an element absorbs or delivers power. If the current enters the terminal marked + and the product VI is positive, the element absorbs power (a resistor, or a battery being charged). If the current enters the − terminal, the element delivers power VI to the rest of the circuit, as a battery does when it discharges. In any complete circuit the power delivered by the sources equals the total power absorbed.

theoryAdd.text: Common mistakes in power and energy problems:
items: Multiplying kW by minutes or seconds and calling the answer kWh; convert the time to hours first.
Using P = V²/R with a resistance found at a different voltage for a non-ohmic lamp; the resistance of a rated lamp is assumed constant only when the question says so.
Adding the ratings of lamps connected in series; for equal-voltage lamps in series the total power is less than that of either lamp alone.
Forgetting efficiency: output power = efficiency × input power, so the input (and the bill) is output ÷ efficiency.
Treating mAh as energy; mAh is charge, and energy in Wh = voltage × Ah.

theoryAdd.text: When a lamp or heater is rated P watts at V volts, first find its resistance R = V²/P and then work at the actual voltage. At half the rated voltage a fixed resistance takes only one-quarter of the rated power.

questions.questionText: A charge of 30 C passes a point in a conductor in 1 minute. The current is:
To measure the voltage across a circuit element, a voltmeter should be connected:
options: In series with the element, and ideally have zero resistance
In parallel with the element, and ideally have zero resistance
In series with the element, and ideally have infinite resistance
In parallel with the element, and ideally have infinite resistance
questions.explanation: A voltmeter is placed across (in parallel with) the element and should draw no current, so its ideal resistance is infinite. An ammeter goes in series and ideally has zero resistance.

questions.questionText: A 1 kW room heater runs for 30 minutes. The energy it uses is:
questions.explanation: W = Pt = 1 kW × 0.5 h = 0.5 kWh.

questions.questionText: One volt is equivalent to:
questions.explanation: V = W/Q, so 1 V = 1 J/C. A coulomb per second is an ampere and a joule per second is a watt.

questions.questionText: One watt is equal to:
questions.explanation: Power is the rate of doing work, P = W/t, so 1 W = 1 J/s.

questions.questionText: An appliance draws 4 A from a 230 V supply. The power it takes is:
In the external circuit connected to a battery, conventional current flows:
options: From the negative terminal to the positive terminal, with the electron flow
From the positive terminal to the negative terminal, with the electron flow
From the positive terminal to the negative terminal, opposite to electron flow
questions.explanation: Conventional current is the direction positive charge would move: from + to − outside the source. Electrons actually move from − to +.

questions.questionText: The terminal voltage of a practical battery is equal to its EMF when:
options: No current is drawn from it
questions.explanation: V = E − Ir, so V = E only when I = 0 (open circuit). On short circuit the terminal voltage falls to zero.

questions.questionText: A motor has an output rating of 5 hp. Taking 1 hp = 746 W, its output in kilowatts is:
Which of the following is a unit of power?
questions.explanation: The horsepower (746 W) measures power. The kilowatt-hour and the joule are units of energy and the coulomb is the unit of charge.

questions.questionText: The resistance of a 60 W, 240 V lamp at its rated operating condition is:
One electron-volt (eV) is:
options: The charge on one electron, about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C
The energy gained by one electron moving through a potential difference of 1 V, about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
The potential difference needed to move one electron, 1 V
The power used by one electron in 1 second
questions.explanation: W = QV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C × 1 V = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; the electron-volt is a unit of energy.

questions.questionText: A 2 kW heater is used for 4 hours. At a tariff of Rs 12 per unit (kWh), the cost is:
questions.explanation: Energy = 2 kW × 4 h = 8 kWh; cost = 8 × 12 = Rs 96.

questions.questionText: The energy needed to move a charge of 5 C through a potential difference of 9 V is:
A battery supplies a steady current of 5 A for 2 hours. The total charge delivered is:
A current of 1.6 mA flows for 1 second. Taking the electron charge as 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the number of electrons passing any section of the conductor is:
questions.explanation: Q = It = 1.6 × 10⁻³ C, so N = Q/e = 1.6 × 10⁻³ / 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 10¹⁶ electrons.

questions.questionText: A copper wire of cross-section 1 mm² carries a current of 1 A. Taking the free-electron density n = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³ and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the drift velocity of the electrons is approximately:
questions.explanation: v = I/(nAe) = 1 / (8.5 × 10²⁸ × 10⁻⁶ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) ≈ 7.35 × 10⁻⁵ m/s, a fraction of a millimetre per second.

questions.questionText: Electrons drift through a wire at well under a millimetre per second, yet a lamp several metres away lights almost as soon as the switch is closed. This is because:
options: Electrons leave the battery at nearly the speed of light
The lamp stores charge and releases it when the switch closes
The current flows only on the surface of the wire
The electric field is set up along the whole circuit almost instantly, so free electrons everywhere start drifting together
questions.explanation: The wire is already full of free electrons. Closing the switch establishes the field throughout the circuit at close to the speed of light, and all the electrons begin to drift at once.

questions.questionText: A battery of EMF 12 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω is connected to a 5.5 Ω load. The terminal voltage of the battery is:
A cell of EMF 1.5 V has an internal resistance of 0.25 Ω. The current it delivers when its terminals are short-circuited is:
questions.explanation: With zero external resistance I_sc = E/r = 1.5/0.25 = 6 A.

questions.questionText: A battery reads 6.0 V on open circuit and 5.4 V when it supplies 3 A to a load. Its internal resistance is:
questions.explanation: The drop inside is 6.0 − 5.4 = 0.6 V, so r = 0.6/3 = 0.2 Ω. (1.8 Ω is the load resistance 5.4/3.)

questions.questionText: A 12 V battery with an internal resistance of 0.1 Ω is being charged at 10 A. The voltage that must be applied across its terminals is:
questions.explanation: While charging, current is forced into the positive terminal against the EMF, so V = E + Ir = 12 + 10 × 0.1 = 13 V.

questions.questionText: A current of 3 A flows through an 8 Ω resistor. The power dissipated is:
questions.explanation: P = I²R = 3² × 8 = 72 W.

questions.questionText: A 48 Ω resistor is connected across a 12 V supply. The power it dissipates is:
A lamp rated 100 W at 230 V is operated from a 115 V supply. Assuming its resistance stays constant, the power it takes is:
questions.explanation: R = 230²/100 = 529 Ω; P = 115²/529 = 25 W. Power varies as V², so half the voltage gives one-quarter of the power.

questions.questionText: A 1 kΩ resistor has a power rating of 0.25 W. The largest DC voltage that can be applied across it continuously without exceeding this rating is about:
questions.explanation: P = V²/R, so V_max = √(PR) = √(0.25 × 1000) ≈ 15.8 V (the corresponding current is 15.8 mA). Multiplying P × R gives 250 V, and √P alone gives 0.5 V.

questions.questionText: Two heaters are rated for the same voltage, one at 500 W and the other at 1000 W. Compared with the 500 W heater, the 1000 W heater has:
questions.explanation: R = V²/P, so at equal rated voltage the resistance is inversely proportional to the power rating: doubling P halves R.

questions.questionText: An energy of 2.5 kWh expressed in joules is:
A motor takes 10 A from a 230 V supply and delivers an output of 2.5 hp (1 hp = 746 W). Its efficiency is approximately:
A 12 V battery is rated at 100 Ah. The energy it can store is:
questions.explanation: Energy = V × charge = 12 V × 100 Ah = 1200 Wh = 1.2 kWh.

questions.questionText: A phone battery has a capacity of 3000 mAh. If the phone draws an average current of 250 mA, the battery will last about:
questions.explanation: Time = capacity/current = 3000 mAh / 250 mA = 12 h.

questions.questionText: A circuit element has 5 V across it, and a current of 2 A enters it at its negative terminal. Using the passive sign convention, the element:
questions.explanation: Current entering the − terminal means the element pushes charge up to the higher potential, so it acts as a source: it delivers P = VI = 5 × 2 = 10 W.

questions.questionText: Which statement about EMF and potential difference is correct?
options: A cell has an EMF even on open circuit, but a potential difference across a resistor exists only while current flows through it
EMF and potential difference are both zero when the circuit is open
The terminal potential difference of a cell on load is always greater than its EMF
EMF is measured in joules and potential difference in volts
questions.explanation: EMF is the energy per coulomb produced by the source and exists without current. A drop across a resistor is IR, so it is zero when I = 0. On load, V = E − Ir is less than E, and both are measured in volts.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a unit of energy?
questions.explanation: The kilowatt is a unit of power. A watt-second is a joule, and the electron-volt and kilowatt-hour are also energy units.

questions.questionText: An ideal current source has:
options: Zero internal resistance, and its terminal voltage is set by the load
Infinite internal resistance, and its current is set by the load
Infinite internal resistance, and its terminal voltage is set by the load
Zero internal resistance and a fixed terminal voltage
questions.explanation: An ideal current source delivers the same current into any load, which needs an infinite parallel (internal) resistance; the voltage across it is whatever the load makes it, V = IR_L.

questions.questionText: A practical voltage source of EMF 10 V with an internal resistance of 2 Ω is converted into an equivalent practical current source. The current source is:
questions.explanation: The equivalent current source has I = E/r = 10/2 = 5 A with the same 2 Ω placed in parallel; both give 10 V on open circuit and 5 A on short circuit.

questions.questionText: An appliance uses 1.8 MJ of energy in 30 minutes. Its power is:
A source has an internal resistance of 1 Ω. For its terminal voltage to be 90% of its EMF, the load resistance must be:
questions.explanation: V/E = R/(R + r) = 0.9 gives R = 0.9R + 0.9, so 0.1R = 0.9 and R = 9 Ω.

questions.questionText: A 1000 W, 250 V heater element is to be wound from nichrome wire 0.5 mm in diameter (ρ = 1.1 × 10⁻⁶ Ω·m). The length of wire required is approximately:
A house uses five 40 W lamps for 6 hours a day, an 80 W fan for 10 hours a day and a 1 kW iron for 1 hour a day. At Rs 9 per unit, the electricity cost for a 30-day month is:
A battery drives 2 A through a 4 Ω resistor and 1 A through a 9 Ω resistor. The EMF and internal resistance of the battery are:
questions.explanation: E = 2(4 + r) and E = 1(9 + r), so 8 + 2r = 9 + r, giving r = 1 Ω and E = 2 × 5 = 10 V.

questions.questionText: A 24 V source with an internal resistance of 2 Ω supplies a 10 Ω load. The efficiency of power transfer to the load is approximately:
A lamp rated 6 V, 3 W is to be run at its rated condition from a 12 V supply by connecting a resistor in series. The resistor value and the power it dissipates are:
questions.explanation: Lamp current I = P/V = 3/6 = 0.5 A. The resistor drops 12 − 6 = 6 V, so R = 6/0.5 = 12 Ω and P = VI = 6 × 0.5 = 3 W.

questions.questionText: A 100 W lamp and a 60 W lamp, both rated for 230 V, are connected in series across a 230 V supply. Assuming constant resistances, the total power drawn is:
The current in a conductor rises uniformly from 0 to 10 A in 4 s. The charge that passes through the conductor during this time is:
questions.explanation: Charge is the area under the current-time graph: Q = ½ × 4 s × 10 A = 20 C (the average current 5 A for 4 s).

questions.questionText: A 1 kW electric kettle with an efficiency of 80% heats 1.5 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C. Taking the specific heat of water as 4200 J/(kg·°C), the time taken is approximately:
questions.explanation: Heat needed = 1.5 × 4200 × 80 = 504 kJ; electrical input = 504/0.8 = 630 kJ; t = 630 000 J / 1000 W = 630 s = 10.5 min.

questions.questionText: An electric pump raises 1000 kg of water through a height of 20 m in 2 minutes. The overall efficiency of the motor-pump set is 75% and it runs from a 230 V supply. Taking g = 9.81 m/s², the current drawn is approximately:
